title: MemKraft v0.6–v0.8 Dev Notes
summary: The story of how MemKraft expanded from connecting channels, work context, and the memories of multiple agents to include fact validity periods, memory tiers, restorable decay, and file relationship networks.
content:
MemKraft is an integrated memory system for AI agents that I started building because I needed it myself. The more you talk with it, the smarter it gets on its own. A few days ago, I shared the development notes for v0.2–v0.5.
Since then, I’ve made three more updates. This time, the nature of the problem shifted from “the memory held by one agent” to “memory shared by multiple agents,” and from “what we know to be true now” to “when it was true.”
All I did was have a few dozen chats with my first agent, Jeon, here and there in the time I had left. The fourth version, v0.8, went from coding to PyPI release in 9 minutes and 17 seconds. A newly released Opus 4.7 agent completed four features, 83 tests, documentation updates, the build, upload, commit, and push all in one go.
Here are the keywords for each version.
--
v0.6: Where did the memory happen?
Every time you open a new session, the agent starts with a blank slate. What was discussed in yesterday’s Telegram group chat, which iteration the current task is on, what tone I prefer—all of it had to be explained again. That was the starting point for v0.6. Memory isn’t just the content. It also needs to store where it happened, what was being done, and who it was with.
I set up three axes: channel context, task continuity, and agent working memory. Channel context builds up preferences and recent topics for each chat room. Telegram DMs have their own tone, and group chats have their own rhythm. Even for the same question, the answer should change depending on which channel it comes from. Task continuity follows “how far this task has progressed and what comes next” even across sessions. Working memory records, in one line, what each agent is focused on right now, so other agents can avoid duplicate work.
The API was organized around a single function, agent_inject. When delegating work to a sub-agent, it combines the channel, task, and agent state into a Markdown block and injects it into the prompt. An agent starting fresh knows from the first line, “Ah, this is what I was working on in this chat.” The test count went from 328 to 357.
v0.7: Memory is a team sport
Attaching memory to one agent was finished in v0.6, but there are five agents in our house. Jeon, Sion, Mion, Sano, and Raon. They each have different roles, belong to different chat rooms, and sometimes ask me the same thing twice. I wanted to eliminate that waste.
I added the concept of handoffs. When Jeon passes work to Sano, he doesn’t just pass along the task ID. He also sends, as one Markdown block, “the context in which we’ve been working with me so far.” The recipient can continue from the same state. The work delegation chain is recorded too, so you can see at a glance that “this task went from me → Jeon → Sano → Raon.” You can also query, at the channel level, “who is working on what in this chat right now?”
The implementation was simple. I added a few fields to the existing channel and task files, and the handoff function simply combined “my working memory + the selected task state” and appended it to the other agent’s working memory. Still zero external dependencies, all Markdown files. 409 tests. Not a single existing API broke. Starting with v0.7, the work of the five agents became noticeably smoother. There were fewer moments of “I asked Jeon about that earlier—what was it again?”
v0.8: Memory has truth and time too
Up through v0.7, the question was “where is the memory, and who writes it?” v0.8 went one step further: “when was that memory true?” What inspired me were mem0 v3, Letta, and Zep/Graphiti. Each was implementing a temporal knowledge graph in a different way. But all of them required a database. The question for v0.8 was: “Can this be done with only the stdlib, on top of Markdown files?” I tried to answer it by combining four features.
The first is a bitemporal fact layer. Most memory systems record only “A is true now.” But facts in the real world have two time axes: “when was it true?” and “when did we come to know it?” fact_add records a fact together with its validity period, and fact_at retrieves the truth as of a specific date. It is represented as a single line of an inline Markdown comment. Like <!-- valid:[2020-03-01..) recorded:2026-04-17 -->, it becomes the same information whether read by a person or a machine.
The second is memory tiers. I borrowed Letta’s division into core, recall, and archival, but the implementation ends with writing one line, tier: core, in the YAML frontmatter. The working set is automatically assembled from all of core plus recently accessed recall. Without a separate database table, one line at the top of a file distinguishes “this memory needs to be right in front of my mind” from “it’s okay if this stays in the warehouse.”
The third is our own distinction in this version: restorable decay. Other systems implement forgetting as “deletion.” MemKraft implements it as “lowering the weight.” decay_apply pushes a memory toward the back of search results without touching the file. decay_restore can fully restore it at any time. There is also a concept called a tombstone: it is excluded from search but safely stored in the archive directory. Neither mem0, Letta, nor Zep does this. It came from the observation that people don’t completely forget either; things simply become harder to recall.
The fourth is using the filesystem as a graph database. Write [[Simon Kim]] anywhere in a Markdown file, and link_scan automatically indexes the bidirectional link. link_backlinks("Simon Kim") returns every file that mentions Simon Kim, while link_graph returns the N-hop relationship network. It’s similar to Obsidian’s graph view, but the backend is just directories and a few JSON files. stdlib’s re and defaultdict were enough.
The test count went from 409 to 492. I didn’t touch a single line of the existing core code. I attached four new modules in init.py using the mixin pattern, preserving the surgical change principle I’ve followed since v0.5. External dependencies are still zero.
--
The theme running through the three updates from v0.6 to v0.8 was ultimately the expansion of memory’s boundaries. From one to many, from now to when, from content to relationships. Memory is no longer confined to a few files. It expands to include who wrote it, when it was true, and what it is connected to.
Existing agent memory systems each go deep along one axis. MemKraft is still trying to absorb those axes without conflict on a single filesystem. The principle that every storage format should be Markdown and JSON remains intact here too. You should always be able to read it with cat, find it with grep, and dig through it with git log.
